_*This post breaks down several districts with high Latino populations. If you are reading this via email it will most likely cut off early.[We recommend checking out the entire post on The Latino Vote Substack.](https://substack.com/@thelatinovotepodcast)_
| Get more from The Latino Vote Podcast in the Substack app
---|---
Available for iOS and Android
[Get the app](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/7ebae178-1a57-4e3a-ad89-85c379830d59?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
* * *
### The Map is Changing
We begin in Texas, where early voting is underway and turnout numbers from places like Houston, Dallas, and the Rio Grande Valley could preview what 2026 looks like nationwide.
For years, the political establishment treated Latino voters as predictable. That era is over.
Districts that are 30%, 40%, even 80% Latino are now competitive terrain. Congressional control may hinge on places the national media barely understands -- rural South Texas, the Central Valley of California, fast-growing suburbs in Arizona and Colorado, and South Florida.
The "30% rule" that once defined partisan collapse in certain districts is being tested in real time.
* * *
### So What is the 30% Rule?
For twenty years -- from 1990 to 2010 -- there was a quiet rule in California politics: the moment a congressional district hit 30% Latino population, the Republican would lose. Every single time. Like clockwork.
Mike Madrid first documented it. And now, heading into 2026 with a newly redrawn map, that number is showing up again -- across California, Colorado, Arizona, and beyond.
Is the rule still valid in an era of shifting Latino partisanship? We don't pretend to have a clean answer. But if you want to understand where the House majority could flip, you need to understand that number.
* * *
### The Races You Should Be Watching
This is not a national overview. This is a district-by-district breakdown of the congressional races where Latino voters aren't just part of the story -- they are the story. These are the seats that will determine which party controls the House of Representatives, and in each one, the Latino share of the electorate is large enough to be decisive.
Get your pencil out.
#### TEXAS
**TX 28 - 85% Latino |** This is the Henry Cuellar seat, and it's now an R+11 district following redistricting. The most Latino congressional district in the country -- 85% Latino -- is a Republican-leaning seat. That is not a coincidence. It is the story of what's happened to the Latino vote in South Texas over the past decade. Republicans didn't flip this community by accident. They built relationships, ran Spanish-language outreach, and showed up. Whether that hold continues in a year where Latino communities are bearing the brunt of aggressive immigration enforcement is the central question of the 2026 cycle.
| [](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/737dc9d1-6db9-4ec3-ac3e-6855dc6ab1d5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
**TX-15 -- 67% Latino |** Friend of the podcast Bobby Pulido is running for this seat, which is now drawn as an R+12 Trump district. Like TX-28, the numbers here would have been unthinkable to political operatives fifteen years ago. Two-thirds Latino, and leaning Republican. Watch the margins here carefully -- if Democrats are going to make a run at any of the South Texas seats, they'll need to see movement in the underlying numbers first.
| [](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/05e4c3ad-1eb2-4b19-b3c1-c7c3dea079b9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
**TX-34 -- 63%** **Latino** | Vicente Gonzalez holds this seat, which came in at Trump +10 in 2024. Another majority-Latino district that has been trending Republican. Gonzalez is an established incumbent with real roots in the community, but the structural headwinds are significant. Any erosion in Trump's support among South Texas Latinos shows up here first.
| [](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/db79ee31-4dce-405c-aa55-bb4e6cb5b8d7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
**TX-35 -- 38% Latino |** This is the sleeper race on the list. Republicans redrew the old Gregg Casar district, which ran from Austin down through San Antonio along I-35, gutting the liberal Austin base and creating a new seat that is 38-40% Latino, heavily concentrated around San Antonio, and rated R+12. The GOP assumed no Democrat could win it. They may have been wrong. There are multiple Latino candidates on both sides of the primary, including Marine veteran John Lyra on the Democratic side. This is a roll of the dice, and it could be the biggest surprise of 2026.
| [](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/755eb571-94c3-4b1f-a9a8-ed7e7d9da379?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
**TX-33 -- 57% Latino** | The dynamics here make this one of the most analytically interesting races in the country. You have Colin Allred, who spent $31 million on TV running statewide for Senate and represents about half the district, running against Julie Johnson, a white progressive state rep who represents the other 45%, and who has secured endorsements from the entire Democratic House leadership, the Congressional Hispanic Caucus PAC, and every major Latino elected official in Dallas. The question of whether a coalition-endorsed white candidate or a nationally known Black candidate breaks through first tells us something important about how these communities align.
| [](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/4515cbf9-fef7-41cc-b49a-cc5ac2ca54a8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
#### FLORIDA
**FL-27 -- 71% Latino** | This is the Miami seat held by Maria Elvira Salinas, the former Univision anchor turned Republican congresswoman. At 71% Latino, it's one of the highest Latino concentration districts in the country, but the composition matters as much as the number. Roughly 50-55% of those Latinos are Cuban, with growing Venezuelan, Central American, and South American communities making up the rest. Cuban-Americans have been among the most reliable Republican Latino voters in the country -- but cracks are starting to show. Deportations of Cuban nationals under the Trump administration have rattled a community that historically viewed immigration enforcement as someone else's problem. If Cuban support for Republicans slips even 5-10 points, Salinas has a real race on her hands.
| [](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/46b5ed04-86ad-483e-88bb-6da874982cb2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
#### CALIFORNIA
California's redistricting produced a newly drawn map with several districts where Latino population share is at or near the 30% threshold that has historically -- for thirty years -- predicted which party wins the seat. Mike Madrid first documented this rule. It's holding worth watching.
**CA-22 -- 52% Latino** | The David Valadao seat in the Central Valley is the highest-profile California target on this list. It's the most Latino-majority district held by a Republican in Congress, and Valadao has defied conventional wisdom for over a decade by repeatedly winning a seat that on paper shouldn't be winnable for a Republican. Redistricting made it slightly more Democratic. Randy Villegas is the leading Democratic challenger. Mike Madrid's prediction: Valadao loses in 2026. The question is whether Villegas or another Democrat emerges from the primary with enough funding to capitalize.
| [](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/d009226a-989d-433b-a34f-4a2e6b8b2ab4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
**CA-13 -- 41% Latino** | The Adam Gray seat in the Central Valley, running from Stockton down to Modesto, is a different story. Gray is a skilled, moderate Democrat who won the seat in 2024 despite a strong rightward shift among Latinos in the region. Redistricting nudged the seat slightly more Democratic. In a favorable year for Democrats, this should be a lean-Dem hold. The real test comes in a presidential year, when the electorate expands and the Latino shift either reverses or deepens.
| [](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/092b540b-e5c4-4ea8-8a54-f5f2b888b083?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
**CA-47 -- 20% Latino** | David Min's seat in Orange County represents a new kind of competitive district: suburban, multiracial, and college-educated. Orange County Latinos are not farm workers or recent immigrants. They are homeowners, small business owners, and professionals whose voting patterns are more influenced by education and income than by ethnicity. The 20% Latino share is lower than other seats on this list, but the nature of that 20% (more Republican-leaning than in other parts of the state) makes it genuinely swing. This is where the old rulebook doesn't apply.
| [](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/0af26a20-9ea4-41ce-a01c-99daf3b4736e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
**CA-48 -- 30% Latino** | The seat in San Diego that Darrell Issa has held sits right at the magic 30% threshold after redistricting made it slightly more Democratic. It's worth watching not just as a competitive seat, but as a test case for whether the 30% rule still holds in the current political environment.
| [](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/776c0848-e9f2-4644-a3b2-d9f77009ce53?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
#### NEW MEXICO
**NM-2 -- 39% Latino |** Gabe Vasquez holds this seat, and has previously joined the podcast to discuss its Latino population. At 39% Latino in an R+1 or R+2 district, this is a genuine toss-up that requires near-perfect execution from Democrats every cycle. In a good Democratic year, Vasquez should be fine. In a bad one, this is one of the first seats to flip. It's on the board either way.
| [](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/436e3b61-e8a3-458f-88eb-0420921b737c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
#### NEW JERSEY
**NJ-9 -- 30% Latino** | Passaic County, New Jersey, in Nellie Pou's district is not where most people think of when they think of the Latino vote. This seat is 30% Latino, almost entirely Dominican and Puerto Rican, and it's competitive. Chuck did door-knocking work here in 2025 and knows the community well. The diaspora politics here are distinct from anything happening in Texas or California, and the district is worth far more attention than it gets from national political media.
| [](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/f4581d4a-3da0-4cb1-9cea-11758e35b438?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
#### COLORADO
**CO-8 -- 30% Latino** | The seat north of Denver is one of the clearest Democratic pickup opportunities on the map. A Latina congresswoman won the seat four years ago and lost it to Gabe Evans in the 2024 Trump wave. Now a Latino candidate is positioned to win the Democratic primary in a district that sits at the 30% threshold. The suburban Denver Latino community -- more college-educated, more economically secure than many of the communities in other competitive districts -- is a different voting bloc than the ones that dominate the Texas or California conversation. In a strong Democratic year, this should be a flip.
| [](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/7b4f21f6-bc36-445f-86d8-ecaf2bae5d7d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
#### ARIZONA
**AZ-6 -- 20% Latino** | Juan Ciscomani is the Republican Latino incumbent here, and he has become something of a case study in how the GOP can compete for Latino votes when they actually recruit and run Latino candidates. At 20% Latino, the district isn't majority-minority -- but in a close race, every percentage point matters. Democrats have been targeting this seat for two cycles. Whether they find a candidate who can match Ciscomani's personal vote is the question.
| [](https://link.sbstck.com/redirect/de69ae35-b9b3-4883-b014-aec8e9bdf21d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* * *
### A Little History for the Road
Mike drops a history lesson in honor of a date most people let pass without notice: **February 18th, 1946 -- the 80th anniversary of Mendez v. Westminster.**
Eight years before Brown v. Board of Education, a Mexican family in Orange County, California sued their school district for forcing their children into segregated "Mexican schools." The coalition that won that case, consisting of Mexican families, a Japanese family whose land had been seized during internment, the NAACP's Thurgood Marshall filing an amicus brief, is a blueprint for what multiracial political organizing actually looks like.
________________________________________
### This Is Just the Beginning
We're going to spend the next several months going deep on every one of these races. We'll bring candidates in. We'll track early vote. We'll watch the numbers in real time. And when the results come in, we'll tell you exactly what they mean for the future of Latino political power in this country.
**The 2026 Latino Vote Battlefield is set.**

New Episode Out Now -- and the map is more complicated than anyone's telling you. | | , , and | Feb 27 | | | | | ---|---|---|---|--- | | | | | | | | | | | Chuck is back from Oaxaca. Mike is slightly less angry than last week. And the 2026 midterms just got a whole lot more interesting. In the latest episode of The Latino Vote Podcast, " The 2026 Latino Vote Battlefield", dives headfirst into the districts, demographics, and power struggles that will decide control of Congress. And at the center of it all? Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work. Latino voters. Not as a side story. Not as an afterthought. But as the battlefield itself. | | ---|---|--- | | ---|---|--- | | ---|---|--- This post breaks down several districts with high Latino populations. If you are reading this via email it will most likely cut off early. | Get more from The Latino Vote Podcast in the Substack app ---|--- Available for iOS and Android The Map is Changing We begin in Texas, where early voting is underway and turnout numbers from places like Houston, Dallas, and the Rio Grande Valley could preview what 2026 looks like nationwide. For years, the political establishment treated Latino voters as predictable. That era is over. Districts that are 30%, 40%, even 80% Latino are now competitive terrain. Congressional control may hinge on places the national media barely understands -- rural South Texas, the Central Valley of California, fast-growing suburbs in Arizona and Colorado, and South Florida. The "30% rule" that once defined partisan collapse in certain districts is being tested in real time. So What is the 30% Rule? For twenty years -- from 1990 to 2010 -- there was a quiet rule in California politics: the moment a congressional district hit 30% Latino population, the Republican would lose. Every single time. Like clockwork. Mike Madrid first documented it. And now, heading into 2026 with a newly redrawn map, that number is showing up again -- across California, Colorado, Arizona, and beyond. Is the rule still valid in an era of shifting Latino partisanship? We don't pretend to have a clean answer. But if you want to understand where the House majority could flip, you need to understand that number. The Races You Should Be Watching This is not a national overview. This is a district-by-district breakdown of the congressional races where Latino voters aren't just part of the story -- they are the story. These are the seats that will determine which party controls the House of Representatives, and in each one, the Latino share of the electorate is large enough to be decisive. Get your pencil out. TEXAS TX 28 - 85% Latino | This is the Henry Cuellar seat, and it's now an R+11 district following redistricting. The most Latino congressional district in the country -- 85% Latino -- is a Republican-leaning seat. That is not a coincidence. It is the story of what's happened to the Latino vote in South Texas over the past decade. Republicans didn't flip this community by accident. They built relationships, ran Spanish-language outreach, and showed up. Whether that hold continues in a year where Latino communities are bearing the brunt of aggressive immigration enforcement is the central question of the 2026 cycle. | | ---|---|--- TX-15 -- 67% Latino | Friend of the podcast Bobby Pulido is running for this seat, which is now drawn as an R+12 Trump district. Like TX-28, the numbers here would have been unthinkable to political operatives fifteen years ago. Two-thirds Latino, and leaning Republican. Watch the margins here carefully -- if Democrats are going to make a run at any of the South Texas seats, they'll need to see movement in the underlying numbers first. | | ---|---|--- TX-34 -- 63% Latino | Vicente Gonzalez holds this seat, which came in at Trump +10 in 2024. Another majority-Latino district that has been trending Republican. Gonzalez is an established incumbent with real roots in the community, but the structural headwinds are significant. Any erosion in Trump's support among South Texas Latinos shows up here first. | | ---|---|--- TX-35 -- 38% Latino | This is the sleeper race on the list. Republicans redrew the old Gregg Casar district, which ran from Austin down through San Antonio along I-35, gutting the liberal Austin base and creating a new seat that is 38-40% Latino, heavily concentrated around San Antonio, and rated R+12. The GOP assumed no Democrat could win it. They may have been wrong. There are multiple Latino candidates on both sides of the primary, including Marine veteran John Lyra on the Democratic side. This is a roll of the dice, and it could be the biggest surprise of 2026. | | ---|---|--- TX-33 -- 57% Latino | The dynamics here make this one of the most analytically interesting races in the country. You have Colin Allred, who spent $31 million on TV running statewide for Senate and represents about half the district, running against Julie Johnson, a white progressive state rep who represents the other 45%, and who has secured endorsements from the entire Democratic House leadership, the Congressional Hispanic Caucus PAC, and every major Latino elected official in Dallas. The question of whether a coalition-endorsed white candidate or a nationally known Black candidate breaks through first tells us something important about how these communities align. | | ---|---|--- FLORIDA FL-27 -- 71% Latino | This is the Miami seat held by Maria Elvira Salinas, the former Univision anchor turned Republican congresswoman. At 71% Latino, it's one of the highest Latino concentration districts in the country, but the composition matters as much as the number. Roughly 50-55% of those Latinos are Cuban, with growing Venezuelan, Central American, and South American communities making up the rest. Cuban-Americans have been among the most reliable Republican Latino voters in the country -- but cracks are starting to show. Deportations of Cuban nationals under the Trump administration have rattled a community that historically viewed immigration enforcement as someone else's problem. If Cuban support for Republicans slips even 5-10 points, Salinas has a real race on her hands. | | ---|---|--- CALIFORNIA California's redistricting produced a newly drawn map with several districts where Latino population share is at or near the 30% threshold that has historically -- for thirty years -- predicted which party wins the seat. Mike Madrid first documented this rule. It's holding worth watching. CA-22 -- 52% Latino | The David Valadao seat in the Central Valley is the highest-profile California target on this list. It's the most Latino-majority district held by a Republican in Congress, and Valadao has defied conventional wisdom for over a decade by repeatedly winning a seat that on paper shouldn't be winnable for a Republican. Redistricting made it slightly more Democratic. Randy Villegas is the leading Democratic challenger. Mike Madrid's prediction: Valadao loses in 2026. The question is whether Villegas or another Democrat emerges from the primary with enough funding to capitalize. | | ---|---|--- CA-13 -- 41% Latino | The Adam Gray seat in the Central Valley, running from Stockton down to Modesto, is a different story. Gray is a skilled, moderate Democrat who won the seat in 2024 despite a strong rightward shift among Latinos in the region. Redistricting nudged the seat slightly more Democratic. In a favorable year for Democrats, this should be a lean-Dem hold. The real test comes in a presidential year, when the electorate expands and the Latino shift either reverses or deepens. | | ---|---|--- CA-47 -- 20% Latino | David Min's seat in Orange County represents a new kind of competitive district: suburban, multiracial, and college-educated. Orange County Latinos are not farm workers or recent immigrants. They are homeowners, small business owners, and professionals whose voting patterns are more influenced by education and income than by ethnicity. The 20% Latino share is lower than other seats on this list, but the nature of that 20% (more Republican-leaning than in other parts of the state) makes it genuinely swing. This is where the old rulebook doesn't apply. | | ---|---|--- CA-48 -- 30% Latino | The seat in San Diego that Darrell Issa has held sits right at the magic 30% threshold after redistricting made it slightly more Democratic. It's worth watching not just as a competitive seat, but as a test case for whether the 30% rule still holds in the current political environment. | | ---|---|--- NEW MEXICO NM-2 -- 39% Latino | Gabe Vasquez holds this seat, and has previously joined the podcast to discuss its Latino population. At 39% Latino in an R+1 or R+2 district, this is a genuine toss-up that requires near-perfect execution from Democrats every cycle. In a good Democratic year, Vasquez should be fine. In a bad one, this is one of the first seats to flip. It's on the board either way. | | ---|---|--- NEW JERSEY NJ-9 -- 30% Latino | Passaic County, New Jersey, in Nellie Pou's district is not where most people think of when they think of the Latino vote. This seat is 30% Latino, almost entirely Dominican and Puerto Rican, and it's competitive. Chuck did door-knocking work here in 2025 and knows the community well. The diaspora politics here are distinct from anything happening in Texas or California, and the district is worth far more attention than it gets from national political media. | | ---|---|--- COLORADO CO-8 -- 30% Latino | The seat north of Denver is one of the clearest Democratic pickup opportunities on the map. A Latina congresswoman won the seat four years ago and lost it to Gabe Evans in the 2024 Trump wave. Now a Latino candidate is positioned to win the Democratic primary in a district that sits at the 30% threshold. The suburban Denver Latino community -- more college-educated, more economically secure than many of the communities in other competitive districts -- is a different voting bloc than the ones that dominate the Texas or California conversation. In a strong Democratic year, this should be a flip. | | ---|---|--- ARIZONA AZ-6 -- 20% Latino | Juan Ciscomani is the Republican Latino incumbent here, and he has become something of a case study in how the GOP can compete for Latino votes when they actually recruit and run Latino candidates. At 20% Latino, the district isn't majority-minority -- but in a close race, every percentage point matters. Democrats have been targeting this seat for two cycles. Whether they find a candidate who can match Ciscomani's personal vote is the question. | | ---|---|--- A Little History for the Road Mike drops a history lesson in honor of a date most people let pass without notice: February 18th, 1946 -- the 80th anniversary of Mendez v. Westminster. Eight years before Brown v. Board of Education, a Mexican family in Orange County, California sued their school district for forcing their children into segregated "Mexican schools." The coalition that won that case, consisting of Mexican families, a Japanese family whose land had been seized during internment, the NAACP's Thurgood Marshall filing an amicus brief, is a blueprint for what multiracial political organizing actually looks like. This Is Just the Beginning We're going to spend the next several months going deep on every one of these races. We'll bring candidates in. We'll track early vote. We'll watch the numbers in real time. And when the results come in, we'll tell you exactly what they mean for the future of Latino political power in this country.
